passage:
Lalit Uncle from the third floor stood at the lift, shaking out his umbrella. “Whoa, it's raining cats and dogs out there!”
Five-year-old Chaitanya, waiting beside his mother, ran to the window at the end of the corridor and pressed his face to the glass. He looked up at the sky, then down at the car park. “Where are the cats?” he asked. “Uncle, where are the dogs?”
Lalit laughed, then crouched. “I mean it's raining very, very hard. No animals, only water.”
“Oh.” Chaitanya nodded. “Then say it's raining very hard.”

qa.q: What did Lalit Uncle say it was raining?
qa.a: He said it was raining cats and dogs.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya thinking when he looked at the car park and asked where the cats were?
qa.a: He took the words as literally true and expected to see animals, and his looking up and then down shows he was honestly searching. He might also have found the idea funny and wanted to check.

qa.q: What would help a child who takes words at face value?
qa.a: Say plainly what you mean, like “it's raining very hard”, and explain a saying when he asks, as Lalit did.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt when Chaitanya asked about the dogs?
qa.a: Probably amused at first, then a little surprised that the boy took it seriously. His crouching and plain explanation show he respected the question.

grounding: A young child takes raining cats and dogs literally; plain language is clearest.

passage:
“Hemant, keep an eye on the milk for a second,” said Omkar Bhaiya, hurrying to answer the phone.
Hemant stood in the kitchen doorway and stared at the pot, eyes wide, hardly blinking. A minute passed. “Bhaiya!” he called. “My eye is on it but it's going up!”
Omkar rushed back and switched off the flame just as the foam reached the rim. “I meant watch it, Hemant.”
“I did watch it.”
“Sorry, yaar. I should have said: tell me when the milk starts rising.”
“Oh! Okay. It's rising now.”

qa.q: What did Omkar Bhaiya ask Hemant to keep an eye on?
qa.a: He asked him to keep an eye on the milk.

qa.q: What was Hemant thinking when he called that his eye was on the milk?
qa.a: He believed he was doing exactly what he was asked, and was puzzled that the milk still rose. He may also have worried that he had failed.

qa.q: What could Omkar say instead next time?
qa.a: He could say plainly what he wants, like “tell me when the milk starts rising”.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel when he sees the foam?
qa.a: Rushed and a bit annoyed for a moment, then apologetic once he realises the mistake was in his words.

grounding: A young child takes keep an eye on it literally; direct language is clearest.

passage: Note for the staff room, Monday. Thomas, Nursery B. During tidy-up I told Mahima to “pull your socks up” because she was slow. She stopped, bent down and carefully pulled up both socks, then looked at me, waiting. A few children laughed. Mahima's eyes filled. She had done exactly what I said. I knelt and told her, “You're right, you did it. I used a grown-up saying. I meant: please tidy faster.” She nodded and picked up the blocks. Note to self and team: at this age, say what we mean in plain words.

qa.q: What did Mahima do when told to pull her socks up?
qa.a: She bent down and carefully pulled up both socks.

qa.q: Why did Mahima's eyes fill when the children laughed?
qa.a: She probably felt confused and embarrassed, because she had done exactly what she was told and could not see what was funny.

qa.q: What did Thomas do to repair the mix-up?
qa.a: Thomas admitted using a grown-up saying and restated it in plain words, so Mahima knew what was meant and felt right, not silly.

qa.q: How did the laughing children see Mahima's socks?
qa.a: They saw a funny mistake, perhaps because they already knew the saying, without seeing that Mahima had listened carefully.

grounding: Shows a young child taking a saying at face value, and a teacher switching to plain, direct words.

passage: Elizabeth Chechi had to run to the well. “Rafiq, keep an eye on the goat, okay?” When she came back with the pot, Rafiq was crouched nose to nose with the goat, one eye squeezed shut, the other wide open and nearly touching its fur. Behind him, the goat was munching her marigolds. “Rafiq!” He jumped up, puzzled and hurt. “I kept my eye on it! Like you said!” Elizabeth set the pot down and laughed, then stopped. “You did. My mistake. I should have said: watch the goat and don't let it eat the flowers.”

qa.q: What was the goat eating?
qa.a: The goat was munching Elizabeth's marigolds.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when Elizabeth shouted his name?
qa.a: He felt puzzled and hurt, because he believed he had done exactly as told by keeping his eye on the goat.

qa.q: What lesson did Elizabeth take about talking to Rafiq?
qa.a: That plain, direct words work best for him, like saying watch the goat and don't let it eat the flowers.

qa.q: What is it like for Elizabeth to come back and see the marigolds?
qa.a: She is annoyed at first, but seeing Rafiq's hurt face she realises her own words caused the mix-up.

grounding: Shows a young child taking the words keep an eye on literally, and an adult realising plain language is clearest.

passage: Rain hammered the windows of the flat in Manchester. Rosa, the neighbour, came in shaking her umbrella. “Goodness, it's raining cats and dogs out there!” Tariq ran to the window and pressed his hands on the glass, searching the street. “Where? I can't see any!” He checked the sky, the bins, the bus stop. His lip began to wobble. “Are they hurt?” Rosa knelt beside him. “Oh, no cats, no dogs. It's a funny way of saying it's raining very hard.” Tariq frowned. “Then say raining very hard.” “Fair enough,” said Rosa.

qa.q: Where did Tariq look for the animals?
qa.a: Tariq checked the sky, the bins and the bus stop.

qa.q: Why did Tariq's lip begin to wobble?
qa.a: He felt worried that real cats and dogs were out in the storm and might be hurt, because he took Rosa's words at face value.

qa.q: What would help Tariq most when adults use sayings like this?
qa.a: Saying the plain meaning, or explaining the saying straight away, so he isn't left searching for animals.

qa.q: If you were Rosa, what would you want to remember?
qa.a: That young children hear words exactly, so a plain sentence like raining very hard is clearest.

grounding: Shows a young child taking an idiom about rain literally, and why plain, direct words suit this age.

passage:
"Oof, it's raining cats and dogs out there," said Hafsa Miss, shaking her umbrella in the classroom doorway.

Vishal's head snapped up. He climbed onto the bench and pressed his nose to the window, scanning the puddles. "Where? I can't see any puppies."

A few children giggled. Hafsa Miss came and looked out with him. "You're right, there aren't any. It's a funny saying. It just means it is raining very, very hard."

Vishal frowned at the rain. "Then why didn't you say that?"

"Good point," she laughed.

qa.q: What was Vishal looking for in the puddles?
qa.a: Puppies; he said, "I can't see any puppies."

qa.q: What does Vishal's frown and "Then why didn't you say that?" suggest?
qa.a: He feels puzzled and a little annoyed that the words didn't mean what they said, and perhaps embarrassed by the giggles.

qa.q: How can adults make sure a young child like Vishal understands them?
qa.a: Use plain, direct words such as "it is raining very hard", and explain a saying straight away when one slips out.

qa.q: How might Hafsa Miss feel when Vishal asks why she didn't just say that?
qa.a: She finds it funny and fair, as her laugh shows, and it reminds her to speak plainly with little ones.

grounding: It shows a young child taking a saying literally and looking for animals in the rain, and a teacher switching to plain words.
